title: Charge localization to optimize reactant adsorption on KCu7S4/CuO interfacial structure toward selective CO2 electroreduction
abstract: Regulating electronic structure of electrocatalysts to optimize reactant adsorption on the catalyst surface is a crucial tactic to boost catalytic activity in electrocatalysis. Herein, a novel KCu7S4/CuO interfacial structure is well constructed to induce the formation of localized charge region to optimize the adsorption properties of active intermediates at the interface to promote CO2 electroreduction. The catalyst of interfacial catalyst delivered boosted CO2RR activity and selectivity toward formate with a Faraday efficiency (FE) of 71.0 % and a decent current density of 7.56 mA cm 2 at a moderate potential of -0.9 V (versus reversible hydrogen electrode) as well as a good durability. Theoretical calculations unveiled that the enhanced CO2RR activity and formate selectivity could be attributed to the strengthened CO2* adsorption in the initial step, the increased adsorption of the key intermediates OCHO*, and the weakened H* adsorption via the localized positive charge region induced by charge redistribution at interface.

A B S T R A C T
Regulating electronic structure of electrocatalysts to optimize reactant adsorption on the catalyst surface is a crucial tactic to boost catalytic activity in electrocatalysis. The catalyst of interfacial catalyst delivered boosted CO2RR activity and selectivity toward formate with a Faraday efficiency (FE) of 71.0 % and a decent current density of 7.56 mA cm− 2 at a moderate potential of -0.9 V (versus reversible hydrogen electrode) as well as a good durability. sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The consumption of the fossil fuels is unexpectedly soaring along with the increasingly growing of the worldwide carbon dioxide (CO2) accumulation, rapidly spurring the exploitation and utilization of clean energy forms [1]. Nowadays, closing the artificial carbon cycle to achieve carbon neutral is fairly urgent and has become the common goal of the human society for renewable energy storage and environmental sustainability [2]. As an emerging and promising technology, electroreduction of CO2 to valuable chemical feedstocks or fuels not only can reduce CO2 emissions in atmosphere to provide possibility for carbon neutral, but also remedy the intermittent and unstable characteristic of renewable energy resources such as solar, wind and tidal energy [3]. Nevertheless, electrocatalytic CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) still suffers from unsatisfactory activity and selectivity toward target products due to the sophisticated process involving multiple electron transfer, resulting in a wide range of products from C1 (CH4 [4], CH3OH [5], HCOOH [6], CO [3]) to C2+ (C2H4 [7] and C2H5OH [8] etc.). Among the various chemical feedstocks, formate as a liquid fuel is also attached with significant economic value in chemical manufacturing [9]. In
recent studies, the most active Sn [10], Bi [11] and In-based [12] electrocatalysts have shown their significantly boosted performance for CO2RR to formate; precious metal Pd [13] and Ag [14] also presents modest activity for formate production. However, these materials often fall short of industrial standards in some aspects such as selectivity, stability and price [15]. Furthermore, bimetallic sites in alloy are discovered efficient for promoting the activity toward CO2RR to formate due to their particular synergistic effects like orbital interactions [16] and confinement effect [17]. Compared with Bi-based, Sn-based and In-based catalysts toward formate production, Cu-based catalysts possess huge advantage in terms of price. Cu is an earth-abundant element that has an even distribution on the earth and a considerably lower price of ~ $6 kg− 1 [18] than Bi (~ $27 kg− 1) [19], In (~ $240 kg− 1) [20] and Sn (~ $20 kg− 1) [21]. Therefore, significant importance is attached to exploring Cu-based catalysts toward CO2 electroreduction. Recently, researchers have devoted a deal of efforts to fabrications of cheaper Cu-based electrocatalysts for CO2RR to valuable formate, mainly focusing on Cu-based sulfides [22,23], Cu-based bimetal catalyst [24], Cu-based nanostructures integrated with carbon matrix [25,26] and theoretical study on the role of sulfur atom in controlling the

selectivity for formate [27]. However, the product selectivity toward formate for Cu-based CO2RR electrocatalysts is still far from what is expected and the corresponding underlying mechanism of formate formation on Cu-based catalyst surface remains indistinct. Featured with the three-dimensional Cu-S framework enriched with masses of pseudo-one-dimensional ion channels constructed by the K+ cations resident, the structure of KCu7S4 possesses double “CuS3” tetrahedral chains, which lead to 1/4 empty Cu sites, and in turn it endows KCu7S4 relatively high conductivity for electrons and ions [28].
Inspired by the above results, we constructed a strongly coupled interfacial structure of KCu7S4/CuO for efficient CO2 electroreduction to formate. The in situ constructed KCu7S4/CuO directly induced localized charge region, which achieved effective regulations of adsorption of intermediates on the catalyst surface. As thus, the as-prepared composite catalyst displayed a Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 71.0 % toward formate with a decent partial current density of 7.56 mA cm− 2 at a moderate potential of -0.9 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode (vs. RHE), outperforming the counterparts of the individual KCu7S4 microrods and CuO nanosheets. Experimental characterizations and theoretical calculations were conducted to investigate the CO2 adsorption and conversion over the KCu7S4/CuO catalyst, demonstrating that the interfacial structure strengthens the initial CO2 adsorption and the localized positive charge region induced by charge redistribution at the interface can greatly improve the adsorption of the key intermediates OCHO* in the CO2RR, and weaken the H* adsorption to suppress hydrogen evolution. This work presents a new strategy of establishing a localized positive charge region at the interface of composite catalyst to boost CO2RR performance in aqueous solutions.

sections.heading: 2.1. Materials
sections.text: All chemicals were directly used without any further purification. Copper (II) chloride dihydrate (CuCl2⋅2H2O, ≥ 99.9 %) and Nafion solution (5.0 wt.%) was purchased from Aladdin. Potassium hydroxide (KOH, ≥ 85 %), sublimed sulfur (S), absolute ethanol, hydrazine hydrate (N2H4⋅H2O, 85 wt.%), hydrogen peroxide (H2O2, 30 wt.%), dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, ≥ 99.5 %), and formic acid (88 wt.%) were purchased from Sinopharm China.

sections.heading: 2.2.1. Fabrication of KCu7S4 microrods
sections.text: In a typical synthesis of KCu7S4 microrods, 342 mg CuCl2⋅2H2O, 160 mg S and 6 g KOH were displaced into deionized water/absolute ethanol (20 mL/4 mL) mixture, followed by the addition of 2 mL N2H4⋅H2O after complete dispersion. After continuous stirring for 20 min, the suspension was transferred to a 50 mL Teflon-lined stainless steel autoclave and sealed immediately, and the autoclave was maintained in an oven at 150 ◦C for 12 h. After cooling down to room temperature naturally, the black precipitate was obtained and washed with deionized water and absolute ethanol several times, respectively, and then was dried at 60 ◦C overnight.

sections.heading: 2.2.2. Construction of KCu7S4/CuO interfacial structure
sections.text:
To construct the KCu7S4/CuO interfacial structure, in situ oxidation treatment of KCu7S4 was realized via a simple hydrothermal method taking H2O2 as the oxidizing agent. Typically, 50 mg KCu7S4 was dispersed into 20 mL KOH solution (0.1 M) and then 2 mL H2O2 solution was added. After continuous stirring for 20 min, the suspension was transferred to a 50 mL Teflon-lined stainless steel autoclave and sealed immediately, and it was maintained in an oven at 120 ◦C for 3 h. After cooling down to room temperature naturally, the collected precipitate was washed and dried accordingly. For contrast, the hydrothermal time was adjusted to 1 h, 6 h and 10 h to control the proportion of KCu7S4 and
CuO; in addition, the reaction time was also prolonged to 24 h to obtain the individual CuO.

sections.heading: 2.3. Material characterizations
sections.text: The crystalline phase of the as-prepared samples was confirmed by powder X-ray diffraction (XRD, X’pert Pro, Philips; Cu Kα, λ=0.15406 nm). The morphology of the samples was checked with filed-emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM, SU8010, Hitachi) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Tecnai G2 F30, FEI) equipped with energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). The chemical states of surface/subsurface and surface valence band photoemission of the samples were analyzed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, AXIS Ultra DLD-600W, Kratos; Al Kα (1486.6 eV)). Ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) spectra were collected with a He discharged lamp (He I 21.22 eV, Kratos; experimental resolution of 0.15 eV), and the bias voltage of the samples was set to be − 10 V. Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) surface area and the corresponding pore size distribution were measured on a Micromeritics ASAP 2020 sorptometer using nitrogen adsorption/desorption at 77 K.

sections.heading: 2.4. Electrochemical characterizations
sections.text: All electrochemical measurements were conducted in a threeelectrode H-type cell linked with a CHI 760E electrochemical workstation (Chenhua, Shanghai). In the test system, a Nafion 117 proton exchange membrane (PEM) was used to separate the two chambers, a Pt plate and Ag/AgCl (saturated with 3.0 M KCl) served as the counter electrode and reference electrode, respectively, a 1.0 × 1.0 cm2 carbon paper coated with catalysts (with a mass loading of ca. 1.0 mg cm− 2) was taken as the working electrode, and 0.1 M KHCO3 solution (saturated with CO2 or Ar) was employed as the electrolytes (60 mL electrolyte was used to fill each compartment with 40 mL headspace). All polarization curves were collected at a scan rate of 5 mV s− 1. The electrolysis was conducted under various constant potentials to estimate the product compositions at each specific potential. Prior to test, a flow of 20 mL min− 1 CO2 or Ar was continuously poured into the electrolyte for at least half an hour, and it was maintained over the entire electrolysis process. Effective electrochemical active surface area was evaluated by the electrochemical double-layer capacitance (EDLC) values derived from the formula Cdl = Δj/2v, where Cdl, Δj and v are the EDLC (F cm− 2) of the catalysts, current density differences (mA cm− 2) and the scan rate (mV s− 1). All potentials in this work were calibrated according to the equation: ERHE = EAg/AgCl + 0.059 pH + 0.197 V. For the preparation of the working electrode, 10 mg catalyst was dispersed in 980 μL absolute ethanol followed with addition of 20 μL Nafion solution (5.0 wt.%) and the mixture was sonicated for 40 min. to form a homogeneous ink. Next, 100 μL in. was drop-casted on the carbon paper and dried under an infrared lamp for use.

sections.heading: 2.5. Product analysis
sections.text:
The generated gaseous and liquid products of CO2RR were measured by online gas chromatography (GC, GC2030plus, Tet) and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR, Varian, 600 MHz), respectively. Prior to the measurements, the two instruments were calibrated with standard gases or liquid solutions. The preparation of the liquid configuration for NMR measurement is described below. Typically, 400 μL electrolyte was mixed with 100 μL D2O and 5 μL DMSO solution containing 1000 ppm (volume fraction). Thereinto, DMSO was taken as an internal standard. The FE of gas and liquid products at a given potential was calculated according to the following Eqs. (1) and (2), respectively:
FEgas = (NH × n1 × F) / Q × 100%
= (NH × n1 × F) / (Itotal × t × R × T) × 100% (1)
L. Lv et al.
Applied Catalysis B: Environmental 298 (2021) 120531
NH: the number of transferred electrons for gas product formation, which is 2 for H2; F: Faradaic constant, 96485 C mol− 1; P: 1.013 × 105 N m2; V: the gas flow rate measured by a digital flow controller under ambient pressure, 20 mL min− 1; ν (vol%): volume concentration of the generated gas from the cathodic compartment; Itotal: the measured steady-state current; t: time, 60 s; R: molar gas constant, 8.314 N m K-1; T: Kelvin temperature, 298.15 K; n1: the mole number of the gas product; Q: total quantity of electricity passed through the system during the sampling.
FEliquid = (NF × n2 × F) / Q × 100%
= (NF × n2 × F) / (Itotal × t × R × T) × 100% (2)
NF: the number of transferred electrons for liquid product formation, which is 2 for HCOOH; n2: the mole number of the liquid product.

sections.heading: 2.6. Theoretical calculations
sections.text:
First-principles calculations were performed based on density functional theory (DFT) with Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP) [29,30]. The ion-electron interaction is described with the Projector Augmented Wave (PAW) method, the exchange correlation function is described by the Perdew, Burke, and Ernzerhof (PBE) version of the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) [31]. The energy cut-off for the plane-wave basis was set to 500 eV for all calculations. Conjugated gradient method was used to the geometry optimization, the maximal force on each atom was less than 0.05 eV/Å is set as the convergence condition, and the convergence condition for energy is 10− 4 eV. All constructions possess a vacuum region (larger than 20 Å) to prevent interaction between adjacent image cells. The Monkhorst Pack [32] sampling schemes were set of 4 × 2 × 1 for geometry optimization, 6 × 3
× 1 electronic self-consistency, respectively. The calculation method for electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 to HCOOH is based on the previously reported literatures [33].

sections.heading: 3.1. Catalyst synthesis and characterizations
sections.text:
The construction of the KCu7S4/CuO composite was achieved by two-step sequential hydrothermal methods, as illustrated in Fig. 1a. Firstly, KCu7S4 microrods were synthesized as the precursor. Then H2O2 solution was employed as an oxidizing agent to convert partial sulfides at the surface of KCu7S4 microrods to construct the KCu7S4/CuO interfacial structure, and the oxidation degree was controlled by the reaction time. Notably, individual CuO nanosheet-assembled microrods could be obtained when the oxidation was prolonged to 24 h (which can be verified by following XRD characterization). The microstructures of the as-prepared samples were characterized by FESEM to verify morphology evolution following oxidation treatment of KCu7S4 microrods. As shown in Figs. 1b and S1a–b, it can be observed that the as-prepared KCu7S4 displays microrod-like morphology and smooth surface with a rectangular cross-section and the width of these microrods is about 1.0 μm. After the in-situ oxidation treatment of the sulfide mirorods, the smooth surface of the microrods is covered with dense CuO nanosheets, thus forming KCu7S4/CuO core-shell interfacial structure. The KCu7S4/CuO interfacial structure integrally inherits the microrod-like morphology of its precursor with the width almost unchanged (as shown in Fig. 1c), and the grown CuO exhibits uniform nanosheet morphology with the thickness of 30− 50 nm (in the inset of Fig. 1c). After thoroughly oxidized, the sulfide-oxide interfacial structure totally turns into CuO without sulfide residues, and the integral microrod morphology is retained without collapse while the distribution of nanosheets becomes
L. Lv et al.
Applied Catalysis B: Environmental 298 (2021) 120531
more compact and denser, and no obvious change is found regarding the thickness of the nanosheets (presented in Fig. S2a–b). Apart from the morphology evolution resulted from oxidation treatment, the elemental composition of the precursor KCu7S4 also varied along with treatment time (in Fig. S3). The TEM and the corresponding elemental mapping images were collected to further investigate the microstructure and elemental distribution/composition. As shown in Fig. 1d, the KCu7S4/ CuO core-shell structure featured with a KCu7S4 microrod backbone on which numerous CuO nanosheets grows can be clearly observed. From the enlarged picture, it can be determined that the grown CuO nanosheets possess the thickness of less than 50 nm, ensuring that plenty of active sites can participate in the CO2RR process. A HRTEM image was recorded (Fig. 1f) at the interface of the KCu7S4/CuO, two disparate divisions were apparently examined (separated with a yellow dash line). The corresponding interplanar spacings were measured to be 0.18 nm and 0.26 nm, indexing with KCu7S4 (440) and CuO (1 11) planes. Selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern reflects multiple concentric circles, corresponding to (1 11), (200), (020), (220), (1 31) and (313) planes of CuO with monoclinic phase, indicating its polycrystalline feature. To further prove this point, we also captured some lattice fringes of CuO nanosheets from another region (as shown in Fig. S4), and the interplanar spacings were measured to be 0.28 nm and 0.26 nm, corresponding to the (110) plane and (1 11) plane of CuO with monoclinic structure, further demonstrating its polycrystalline structure. Concerning some conspicuous bright spots in Fig. 1g, the corresponding interplanar spacings were measured to be 0.23 nm, 0.19 nm and 0.14 nm, ascribed to the (420), (002) and (631) planes of tetragonalphase KCu7S4. These discussions are in well agreement with the XRD results. The elemental distribution and composition of KCu7S4/CuO was further validated by TEM energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (TEMEDS). A high-angle annular dark field scanning transmission electron microscope (HAADF-STEM) image and the corresponding elemental mapping were captured as shown in Fig. 1h. It is confirmed that K, Cu, S and O elements indeed exist in the interfacial structure. The TEM-EDS spectrum reveals the elemental composition of KCu7S4/CuO, and the peaks for Mo are ascribed to the TEM grid (Fig. S5). Noticeably, it can be distinguished that K, and S elements are evenly distributed on the backbone, while O element is mainly dispersed on the branch, namely the shell, demonstrating the tight coupling of the two components, i.e., KCu7S4 and CuO.
The crystalline structures of the as-prepared samples were clarified by XRD. As shown in Fig. 2, in the XRD pattern of the precursor KCu7S4 microrods, six strong peaks located at 12.3◦, 27.7◦, 35.3◦, 43.6◦, 50.8◦
and 54.2◦ were observed, which could be indexed to the (110), (310), (400), (411), (440) and (600) planes of tetragonal-phase KCu7S4 (JCPDS # 47-1334). After the oxidation treatment for 3 h, the intensities of peaks for KCu7S4 were sharply weakened, and the arresting peaks at 35.5◦, 38.7◦, 48.7◦, 61.6◦, 66.2◦ and 68.1◦ could be found, attributing to the (1 11), (111), (2 02), (1 13), (311) and (220) planes of CuO with monoclinic structure (JCPDS # 05-0661). When the thorough oxidation was carried out, the peaks for KCu7S4 disappeared and all peaks belonged to monoclinic CuO. To disclose the crystal structure evolution, the XRD patterns of all KCu7S4/CuO composites derived from oxidation treatment of different time were also provided (Fig. S6). XPS was performed to reveal the chemical valence states of the as-prepared KCu7S4 and KCu7S4/CuO. The XPS survey spectrum of KCu7S4 evidences the existence of K, Cu, S and O (Fig. S7). In the Cu 2p core-level spectrum of KCu7S4 (Fig. 3a), a pair of strong peaks at 932.2 eV (Cu 2p3/2) and 952.1 eV (Cu 2p1/2) is deconvoluted, ascribing to monovalent Cu(I); while another pair of strong peaks at 934.2 eV (Cu 2p3/2) and 953.8 eV (Cu 2p1/2) are deconvoluted, accompanying with three satellite peaks, associating with Cu(II) [34,35]. It is worth noting that the Cu 2p3/2 peak in the Cu 2p core-level spectrum of KCu7S4/CuO is positively shift by ~0.50 eV compared with that of the individual KCu7S4, which unequivocally corroborates the strong electron interactions between KCu7S4 and CuO in the as-fabricated KCu7S4/CuO composite [36,37]. The positive shift of Cu 2p3/2 peak suggests that partial charge is depleted and transferred from KCu7S4 to CuO, thus spontaneously forming localized positive sites (Cu(1+δ)+, 0< δ < 1) in the KCu7S4 section at the interface, which in turn strengthens the adsorption of O-bound *OCHO intermediate and accelerating the formation of formate [38]. In the S 2p core-level spectrum, a pair of peaks at 161.3 eV and 162.4 eV for S 2p3/2 and S 2p1/2 is deconvoluted, affirming the formation of KCu7S4 [39]. Regarding the O 1s spectrum, two peaks at 529.6 eV and 531.1 eV are deemed as lattice oxygen (Olatt) in CuO and adsorbed oxygen (Oads) on the catalyst surface [40,41]. To further unveil the interactions between KCu7S4 and CuO in the interfacial structure, UPS spectra of the three samples were collected (as shown in Fig. S8) to derive their work functions. According to the formula: φ = hv + ECutoff - EFermi (φ is the work function, hv is the energy of excitation source, ECutoff and EFermi are the energies of cutoff side and Fermi side, respectively), it is calculated that the individual KCu7S4 delivers a lower work function of 7.481 eV than that of the individual CuO (8.127 eV), while the interfacial catalyst KCu7S4/CuO possesses the lowest work function of 6.832 eV among them, demonstrating the strong interactions between KCu7S4 and CuO at the interface, namely, electrons could transfer from KCu7S4 to CuO [42]. N2 adsorption/desorption measurements were carried out to detect the porous structure of the samples. As shown in Figs. 3d and S9, distinct hysteresis loops at relative pressure (P/P0) for all the three samples are clearly observed, demonstrating their mesoporous structure. Derived from N2 adsorption/desorption isotherm, the Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) surface area and the total pore volume of the KCu7S4/CuO composite are assessed to be 30.8 m2 g− 1 and 0.152 cm3 g− 1, which is significantly increased compared with those (19.1 m2 g− 1 and 0.042 cm3 g− 1) of the individual KCu7S4. It is well acknowledged that the enhanced BET and pore volume values of the KCu7S4/CuO composite can benefit to the adsorption of CO2 molecules and exposure of adequate active sites, thus promoting the electrochemical CO2RR performance [43]. Besides, it is proposed that the BET and pore volume values approach to those (34.5 m2 g− 1 and 0.156 cm3 g− 1) of the individual CuO, indicating the great contribution of the grown CuO nanosheets on the KCu7S4 backbone to the increased surface area.

sections.heading: 3.2. Electrocatalytic performance for CO2 reduction of the catalysts
sections.text:
The electrocatalytic CO2RR activities of the as-prepared samples were evaluated in a three-electrode H-type cell linked with a CHI 760E electrochemical workstation using CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 solution as the electrolytes. Firstly, the samples were activated by continuous cyclic voltammetry (CV) test in the potential range of 0 ~ -1.2 V (V vs. RHE) at a scan rate of 50 mV s− 1 to obtain stable CV curves (Fig. S10a). The corresponding linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) tests for the three samples, i.e., KCu7S4, KCu7S4/CuO and CuO, were conducted as well in the same potential window, as shown in Figs. 4a and S10b. The cathodic polarization curves indicate that all the three samples are active for CO2RR since the detected currents in CO2 atmosphere are apparently increased compared with those in Ar atmosphere. Whereas the KCu7S4/ CuO composite exhibits the largest current density of 21.1 mA cm-2 at the potential of 1.2 V, surpassing the individuals KCu7S4 (19.5 mA cm-2) and CuO (18.3 mA cm-2). Nevertheless, the measured current density is not absolutely contributed from CO2RR activity due to the existence of inescapable and competitive HER in aqueous solution. To notarize the contribution of preferential CO2RR and exclude the partial current density generated by HER, amperometric i–t tests (Fig. S11) were performed at various constant potentials for the samples to detect all products. During the electrolyses, gaseous and liquid products were quantificationally measured by GC and NMR, respectively, and the results revealed that only H2 and formate were detected throughout all constant potentials. Remarkably, the one-dimensional KCu7S4 mirorods possess a better CO2RR performance than the commercial Cu2S (denoted as c-Cu2S), indicating the structural advantage featured with the threedimensional Cu-S framework enriched with masses of pseudo-one-
dimensional ion channels constructed by the K+ cations resident (in Fig. S12) [28]. It is obviously observed that the KCu7S4/CuO is the most favorable for formate formation among all the samples in a wide potential range (from − 0.7 to − 1.2 V) with a maximum FE of 71.0 % at the potential of -0.9 V (corresponding to a decent partial current density of 7.56 mA cm-2) without ohmic resistance compensation (Fig. 4b), surpassing those of KCu7S4 (46.9 %), CuO (32.9 %) and c-Cu2S (37.9 %). Fig. 4c exhibits the partial current density toward formate (jformate) of the KCu7S4, KCu7S4/CuO and CuO transformed by total j in potentiostatic mode and the corresponding FE. It is conspicuous that the KCu7S4/CuO delivers high catalytic activity for CO2RR toward formate formation, reaching a high jformate of about 15.43 mA cm-2 at a moderate potential of -1.2 V, which exceeds the counterparts of other catalysts (about 8.47 mA cm-2 for KCu7S4 and 3.09 mA cm-2 for CuO). Moreover, it can be found that the formate formation has already started on KCu7S4/CuO with the jformate of 1.40 mA cm-2 at a low potential of -0.7 V, approaching to the theoretical equilibrium potential of -0.17 V [44].
To gain mechanistic insights into the kinetics of CO2RR to formate over the electrocatalysts from the perspective of electrochemical analysis, a Tafel plot (Log [jformate] versus potential, with ohmic resistance compensation) was converted from the correlation of potential and current density (as shown in Fig. 4d). It is distinct that the KCu7S4/CuO exhibits a Tafel slope of 188 mV dec− 1, much smaller than that of the individual KCu7S4 (226 mV dec− 1) and more closes to the theoretical value of 118 mV dec− 1 for formate formation [45], suggesting that the two catalysts undergo different CO2RR mechanisms. The KCu7S4/CuO possesses a fast 1e- pre-equilibrium transfer to form CO2⋅- anion radical prior to a chemical H+ transfer step while the KCu7S4 proceeds an initial rate-limiting 1e- transfer from CO2 to CO2⋅- that needs higher
L. Lv et al.
Applied Catalysis B: Environmental 298 (2021) 120531
overpotentials [46]. The number of catalytically active sites is highly related to the catalytic activity and product selectivity. Hence, the double layer capacitance was measured to determine the electrochemically active surface area (ECSAs) of the catalysts (Fig. S13). Fig. 4e revealed that the Cdl (14.6 m F cm-2) of the KCu7S4/CuO increased after constructing the interfacial structure (10.8 m F cm-2 for the KCu7S4), evidencing the enhanced number of active sites via interface engineering. Figs. 4f and S14 presented the total current density, product composition and the corresponding FE. It can be perceived that the products of CO2RR over the KCu7S4/CuO and the individual KCu7S4 both consist of HCOOˉ and H2; in stark contrast, the products over CuO comprise of HCOOˉ, H2, CO, C2H4 and C2H6. To optimize the reaction time of oxidation treatment, the corresponding FE values toward HCOOˉ and H2 over other KCu7S4/CuO composites with different constitution via oxidation treatment of different time (1 h, 6 h and 10 h) were provided for comparison as well (Fig. S15). Among all the samples, the KCu7S4/CuO derived from oxidation of KCu7S4 for 3 h exhibits the highest FE toward HCOOˉ and the lowest FE toward H2 in the wide potential window, and the maximum FE of 71.0 % toward HCOOˉ is achieved at the potential of − 0.9 V (Fig. 4g), manifesting the outstanding CO2RR performance comparable to those of the reported Cu-based electrocatalysts toward CO2RR to HCOOˉ in previous literatures (Table S1). We further carried out the chronoamperometric test at the potential of -0.9 V as the catalyst stability at low overpotentials is crucial for industrial applications of electrochemical CO2RR. It is observed that the current density and FEformate (Fig. 4h) can be nearly
preserved over 14 h with only 4.0 % dinky degradation of FEformate in the stability test. Evidenced by the XRD pattern and FESEM image (Fig. S16) of the spent KCu7S4/CuO, the inappreciable drop of FEformate may be attributed to the variations of the material structures. In the meantime, XPS spectra (Fig. S17) of the spent sample proved that the sulfide and oxide residues on the catalyst surface/subsurface were still maintained, confirming the origin of the excellent stability of the KCu7S4/CuO for CO2RR.

sections.heading: 3.3. Experimental and theoretical study for catalytic mechanism
sections.text:
To probe the underlying mechanism of the efficient CO2RR to formate and the origin of highly catalytic activity of the KCu7S4/CuO toward CO2RR, we adopted both experimental and theoretical approaches to explore the significant role of the interfacial structure playing in the formate formation process and the enhanced CO2RR activity. According to the previous studies [47,48], it is well acknowledged that the reaction pathways for CO2RR to formate is proposed as follows:
CO2 (g) + e− + ∗ → CO⋅− ∗2 (3)
CO⋅− ∗2 + HCO − 3 + e − →HCOO− ∗ + CO2−3 (4)
HCOO− ∗→HCOO− + ∗ (5)
where * represents the adsorption site on the catalyst surface. The sol-
L. Lv et al.
Applied Catalysis B: Environmental 298 (2021) 120531
ubility of CO2 in aqueous solution is usually limited and the related mass transfer resulted from CO2(aq)/HCO3− /CO32- equilibrium certainly constrains the polarization current during CO2RR [49], hence CO2 adsorption on the catalyst surface in the initial step is of great significance as the prerequisite for CO2RR and the corresponding adsorption intensity determines the kinetics rate of subsequent procedures [48]. As shown in Fig. 5a, CO2 adsorption measurements implemented on the individual KCu7S4 and KCu7S4/CuO indicated that the KCu7S4/CuO possessed a stronger adsorption capability than the individual KCu7S4, suggesting the advantage of the rationally designed interfacial structure toward CO2 adsorption. The surface electronic structure of catalysts which could be determined by E-EF parameter with respect to the Fermi level, generally plays a significant role in regulating catalytic performance as it can greatly affect the bonding strength of intermediates on the catalyst surface [50]. Fig. 5b reveals that the d band centers obviously shift downwards from − 4.05 to − 5.15 eV after establishing the interfacial structure. The down-shift of the d band centers increases the bonding states and decreases the anti-bonding states, weakening the catalyst-adsorbate interaction, especially the adsorption of H* due to its larger coverage on the catalyst surface. Hence, the KCu7S4/CuO exhibited a weaker adsorption of H* than the individual KCu7S4, which favors the suppression of the hydrogen evolution.
To further elucidate the electrocatalytic CO2RR and HER pathways on the catalyst surface, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were adopted to obtain a theoretical understanding on the evident enhancement of CO2RR activity over the KCu7S4/CuO with featured interfacial structure from atomic level. Generally, the constructed interface will induce charge redistribution to create a localized charge region due to the different positions of Fermi energy. As shown in Fig. 6a and b, the individual KCu7S4 possesses a smaller work function of 5.736 eV compared with that of CuO (7.451 eV), leading to the charge transfer from KCu7S4 to CuO, which is in well agreement with the UPS analysis results. Indeed, as evidenced by the differential charge density (in Fig. 6c) and Bader charges, it was calculated that 0.58 e− transferred from KCu7S4 to CuO at the interface. The redistributed local charge can effectively modulate the adsorption energy of intermediates (such as CO2, OCHO* and HCOOH) in the CO2RR process and the positively charged metal sites could enhance the metal-O bonding with OCHO*, which benefits to the formation of formate on the catalyst surface [38]. Furthermore, the d-band center (εd) of the KCu7S4/CuO is more far away from the Fermi level (shown in Fig. 6d), indicating the H-adsorbate is weakened, which is in well agreement with the experimental results. As shown in Fig. 6e, two-step electron-proton coupling transfer steps (including the formation of OCHO* intermediate) are involved for the electrocatalytic CO2RR to HCOOH. For the individual KCu7S4 and KCu7S4/CuO, the electron transfer steps from CO2 to OCHO* require large energy barrier, suggesting the potential-limiting step is the formation of OCHO* [33]. Interestingly, after decorating CuO on the KCu7S4 surface, the Gibbs free-energy difference (ΔG) for H* (the key intermediate for HER) formation apparently increased from 0.78 to 1.32
eV and ΔG for OCHO* formation is visibly decreased, indicating the localized positive charge regions in KCu7S4 counterpart at the interface benefit to the OCHO* intermediate formation and hinder the H* formation. Furthermore, the adsorption energies of intermediate species were also collected to demonstrate the adsorption strength of the interfacial structure for CO2*, OCHO* and HCOOH (shown in Fig. 6f). It is exactly confirmed that the KCu7S4/CuO possesses the more negative adsorption energies for these intermediates, suggesting a stronger binding capability of CO2* and OCHO* on the KCu7S4/CuO catalyst surface. The theoretical calculation results not only verified the underlying mechanism of the enhanced CO2-to-formate conversion efficiency but also navigated for the electrocatalyst design toward formate production.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text:
In summary, the electrocatalytic CO2RR activity toward formate formation was obviously boosted by constructing the interfacial structure composed of KCu7S4 microrod backbones and CuO nanosheet branches. The as-fabricated KCu7S4/CuO catalyst delivered a FE of 71.0 % for formate at the potential of -0.9 V with a decent partial current density of 7.56 mA cm− 2 and a good stability in aqueous electrolytes. The underlying mechanism of CO2-to-formate conversion was unveiled and the newly born active sites were also confirmed by both experimental approaches and theoretical calculations. It is predicatively determined that the enhanced CO2RR performance toward formate formation is mainly attributed to the following two reasons: a) the elaborate interfacial structure strengthens the adsorption of CO2 molecules in the initial step; b) charge redistribution is induced by the two components with different work function to form localized positive charge region, which promotes the adsorption of the key intermediate OCHO* and weakening the adsorption of H* at the interface. It is anticipated that the rationally designed interfacial structure provides a novel strategy to induce the formation of localized charge region for regulating the adsorption properties of intermediates of electrocatalytic CO2RR and pave avenues for the electrocatalyst design in other electrochemical reactions.
